title: Histologic and molecular transformation from non-small cell to small cell lung cancer: insights in the era of expanding treatment options.
authors: Wang Z, Cai G, Zhu J et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with increasing attention being paid to the histologic transformation between non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of NSCLC-to-SCLC transformation, covering the classification of NSCLC subtypes, advances in targeted therapy for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, clinical manifestations of SCLC transformation, diagnostic technologies, therapeutic strategies, ongoing controversies, and future perspectives. By integrating extensive evidence from the literature, we systematically analyze the clinical findings, molecular mechanisms, diagnostic approaches, and treatment modalities related to this phenomenon. Our aim is to offer clinicians and researchers a thorough and insightful reference to facilitate further investigation into NSCLC-to-SCLC transformation and ultimately improve therapeutic outcomes and prognosis for patients with lung cancer.

title: Erlotinib Engineering Programs Tumor Targeting in an Atomically Precise Au8 Cluster.
authors: Wang SB, Ge XY, Xu WH et al.
abstract: Atomically precise metal clusters hold great promise for cancer theranostics, yet current strategies for introducing tumor-targeting functionality often compromise their structural precision. Herein, an erlotinib (Er)-functionalized gold cluster, Au8-Er, is constructed through ligand engineering for targeted non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) theranostics. The Er ligands endow Au8-Er with high affinity toward the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), enabling selective tumor targeting and preferential accumulation at lung tumor sites. Under the glutathione-rich tumor microenvironment, Au8-Er releases Er to achieve chemotherapy. Simultaneously, the cluster exhibits strong X-ray attenuation and oxygen-sensitive phosphorescence, allowing it to function as both an X-ray scintillator and a photosensitizer for efficient X-ray-induced photodynamic therapy (X-PDT) under low-dose irradiation. Moreover, its X-ray-excited luminescence enables high-contrast imaging. The synergistic integration of targeted chemotherapy, X-PDT, and imaging within a structurally precise nanoplatform results in enhanced therapeutic efficacy against NSCLC. This work highlights ligand engineering as an effective strategy for imparting biological functionality to atomically precise metal clusters and advances their application in precision cancer theranostics.

title: Firmonertinib 160mg in EGFR-Mutated NSCLC with Brain Metastases After EGFR-TKI Resistance (iFORCE): Clinical Outcomes and Mechanistic Insights.
authors: You M, Xie T, Wu L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brain metastases (BM) are frequent in EGFR-mutated (EGFRm) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and remain challenging after prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. This exploratory study evaluated high-dose fimmonertinib and explored subtype-specific spatial biology.
METHODS: iFORCE was a prospective, single-center, single-arm study. Eligible patients had advanced NSCLC harboring EGFR mutations with previously treated BM following EGFR-TKI therapy, or intracranial disease progression. Patients received 160 mg firmonertinib once daily. The primary endpoint was intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS). Archival paired primary tumors and BM specimens from an independent retrospective cohort underwent exploratory digital spatial profiling (DSP).
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients were enrolled. At a median follow-up of 19.7 months (95% CI, 14.5-25.3), median iPFS was 14.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-not estimable [NE]), with 12- and 18-month iPFS rates of 53.8% and 46.1%, respectively. Based on the best intracranial overall response, intracranial objective response and disease control rates were 34.8% (95% CI, 16.4-57.3) and 91.3% (95% CI, 72.0-98.9). Median systemic PFS was 10.7 months (95% CI, 3.9-NE). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 13 (56.5%) patients, mostly grade 1; one patient (4.3%) developed grade 3 stomatitis. No treatment discontinuations or treatment-related deaths were observed. DSP revealed distinct EGFR subtype-specific BM ecosystems: exon 19 deletion tumors retained immune-enriched inflammatory programs, whereas L858R-mutated tumors showed tumor-intrinsic cell-cycle, DNA-repair, RNA-splicing, apoptosis-resistance, and immune-evasion features.
CONCLUSIONS: Fimonertinib 160 mg showed promising intracranial activity with a manageable safety profile in EGFR-TKI-treated EGFRm NSCLC with BM. L858R BM displayed tumor-intrinsic, microenvironment-independent biology, suggesting preferential sensitivity to high-dose firmonertinib.

title: Design, synthesis, and anticancer evaluation of Biginelli-derived DHPM-amide hybrids bearing clinically inspired kinase-directed pharmacophores: EGFR docking and DFT studies.
authors: Kothadiya SP, Maheta JB, Lakhnotra DK et al.
abstract: A series of twelve novel dihydropyrimidine (DHPM)-amide hybrid conjugates (6a-c, 8a-c, 10a-c, and 12a-c) were rationally designed, synthesized, and biologically evaluated as potential EGFR-targeted anticancer agents against A549 non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) cells. The target compounds were constructed via a convergent two-step protocol: Biginelli multicomponent condensation to assemble the DHPM-carboxylic acid core (4a-c), followed by EDC·HCl/HOBt-mediated chemoselective amide coupling with four clinically inspired amine fragments derived from erlotinib/gefitinib (series 10), cabozantinib (series 8), imatinib (series 12), and a sorafenib bioisostere (series 6). All compounds were characterized by IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and low-resolution ESI-MS. MTT cytotoxicity screening identified compound 10b as the most potent analogue (IC50 = 16.11 ± 0.11 µg mL-1, equivalent to 23.31 µM), exceeding the molar potency of the reference methotrexate (IC50 = 15.00 ± 0.48 µg mL-1, equivalent to 33.01 µM). It should be noted that methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor included solely as a general cytotoxicity control and is not a mechanistically matched EGFR comparator; the comparison therefore reflects relative cytotoxic potency only and does not imply EGFR selectivity. Molecular docking against EGFR (PDB 1M17), an erlotinib-bound inactive-conformation structure, returned the most favourable score for 10b (score = -7.819 kcal mol-1), with predicted hydrogen bonds to ASP831 and LYS721, a halogen contact at ILE765, and an extensive 15-residue hydrophobic network; these poses indicate compatibility with the erlotinib-binding pocket rather than a confirmed ATP-competitive binding mode. DFT calculations at B3LYP/6-311G(d,p) characterised the electronic structure of the isolated molecule (ΔE = 4.045 eV; ω = 3.155 eV) and are reported as a physicochemical description only, without implying a causal link to cellular activity. Normal mode analysis indicated conformational stability of the 10b-EGFR complex, collectively identifying 10b as a promising lead for further optimisation and mechanistic evaluation, for which direct EGFR kinase assays remain necessary.

title: Multimodality salvage treatment incorporating ivonescimab plus chemotherapy for EGFR-mutated NSCLC with leptomeningeal metastases after dose-escalated third-generation EGFR-TKI failure: a retrospective study.
authors: Wu Q, Qiu L, An J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is among the most devastating modes of progression in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although dose escalation of third-generation EGFR-TKIs has been an important central nervous system (CNS)-directed salvage strategy, therapeutic options after progression on this intensification approach remain limited.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients treated between September 2024 and December 2025. Eligible patients were adults (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, a documented EGFR mutation, and LM diagnosed by gadolinium-enhanced MRI or positive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology. Patients received ivonescimab plus chemotherapy after documented intracranial or extracranial progression on a dose-escalated third-generation EGFR-TKI regimen used for LM management, with or without concurrent CSF-directed therapy. Ivonescimab was given intravenously at 20 mg/kg every 3 weeks with chemotherapy selected according to prior treatment and clinical status. The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) and LM progression-free survival (LM-PFS).
RESULTS: Of 517 screened patients, 33 initiated ivonescimab plus chemotherapy and comprised the overall treated cohort. Concurrent intrathecal or intraventricular chemotherapy was administered to 29 of 33 patients (87.9%). The median age was 61 years (IQR 56-62); 24 (72.7%) were female; 24 (72.7%) had baseline ECOG performance status of 2-3. The median number of prior therapy lines was 4 (IQR 3-6). At a median follow-up of 8.28 months, median OS was 8.54 months (95% CI 5.75-14.32), median LM-PFS was 6.54 months (95% CI 3.42-11.86), and median systemic PFS was 4.83 months (95% CI 2.79-7.56). Three-month treatment persistence was 64.4% (95% CI 44.9-78.6). Among 29 patients evaluable for LM response, 6 achieved a response, yielding an LM response rate of 20.7% (95% CI 8.0-39.7) and an LM disease control rate of 82.8% (95% CI 64.2-94.2). Among 31 patients with evaluable safety documentation, grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 14 (45.2%), most commonly hematologic toxicities. No permanent ivonescimab discontinuation due to toxicity was documented.
CONCLUSIONS: This cohort provides real-world outcome data for patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC and LM receiving multimodality salvage treatment incorporating ivonescimab plus chemotherapy after dose-escalated third-generation EGFR-TKI failure.

title: MMP14-mediated proteolytic cleavage of LAMC2 domain III fragment drives osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Lu CH, Bi WD, Gao ZY et al.
abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a critical clinical challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with 40%-60% of progressing patients lacking an identifiable genetic resistance driver. Through quantitative secretomic profiling of paired osimertinib-sensitive and -resistant NSCLC cell lines, we identified laminin subunit γ2 (LAMC2) as markedly enriched in resistant cell secretomes. Single-cell RNA sequencing reanalysis revealed a LAMC2-high drug-tolerant persister subpopulation that expanded under osimertinib pressure, with pseudotime analysis suggesting progressive co-upregulation of LAMC2 and matrix metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14) along the treatment-to-resistance trajectory. Across four independent cohorts, MMP14 exhibited the strongest co-expression with LAMC2 among all metalloproteinases; the two proteins also physically interacted, and their concurrent high expression predicted the worst overall survival. Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaved LAMC2 to release a bioactive Domain III (DIII) fragment harboring EGF-like repeats, which reactivated EGFR/AKT/ERK signaling despite continued osimertinib exposure. Exogenous DIII conferred resistance in sensitive cells, whereas an anti-DIII blocking antibody reversed MMP14-driven resistance in cell lines and patient-derived organoids. The selective MMP14 inhibitor NSC405020 restored osimertinib sensitivity in vitro and suppressed xenograft growth. In residual tumor tissues from neoadjuvant osimertinib-treated patients, non-responders exhibited higher LAMC2/MMP14 co-expression and more prominent spatial exclusion of CD8⁺ T-cells from the tumor core compared with major pathological responders. These findings identify the MMP14-LAMC2-DIII proteolytic axis as a non-genetic resistance mechanism and suggest that MMP14 inhibition or DIII neutralization may represent a rational strategy to overcome acquired osimertinib resistance.

title: [Variant Allele Frequency Stratification and EGFR Co-mutation Characteristics in AKT1 E17K-mutant Non-small Cell Lung Cancer].
authors: Zhao D, Xie D, Zhang N et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: AKT serine/threonine kinase 1 (AKT1) E17K, the most common activating mutation of AKT1, is an established druggable driver in breast cancer; however, it is exceedingly rare in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with its clinical significance remaining unclear. Variant allele frequency (VAF) may partially reflect the clonal proportion of a mutation, offering clues to the clonal characteristics of such rare mutations. This study investigated the relationship between AKT1 E17K VAF and co-mutation with classic driver genes such as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) in NSCLC, aiming to explore the potential role of this mutation in tumor clonal evolution.
METHODS: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) data of lung cancer patients at Beijing Chest Hospital, Capital Medical University from June 2019 to April 2026 were retrospectively analyzed. After deduplication of 13,003 tests, 11,368 unique patients (including small cell lung cancer) were identified, among whom 35 harbored AKT1 E17K mutations (overall detection rate 0.31%), all being NSCLC; 5 external consultation cases were excluded, leaving 30 cases for analysis. Continuous VAF analysis was designated as the primary analysis, with an exploratory cutoff of 10%.
RESULTS: Of the 30 patients, 20 (66.7%) were adenocarcinoma. Median follow-up was 12 months (range: 1-55 months). The EGFR co-mutation rate was lower in the high-VAF group (≥10%, n=17) than in the low-VAF group (<10%, n=13; 11.8% vs 46.2%), reaching nominal significance before correction [P=0.049, odds ratio (OR)=0.156] but not after Bonferroni adjustment (adjusted P=0.246). The median VAF was lower in the EGFR co-mutated group than in the EGFR wild-type group (1.37% vs 13.73%, P=0.071). Continuous analysis showed a negative trend between VAF and EGFR co-mutation (ρ=-0.340, P=0.066). After adjusting for histological type using Firth-corrected Logistic regression, the direction of the association remained unchanged but was no longer nominally significant (OR=0.21, 95%CI: 0.03-1.33, P=0.097).
CONCLUSIONS: AKT1 E17K VAF showed a negative trend with EGFR co-mutation; however, the association did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons or adjustment for histological type, and may be partly influenced by histological composition. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center cohorts.

title: PLD1-driven oncogenic secretion creates a therapeutic vulnerability in chromosome 3q-amplified NSCLC.
authors: Tan X, Wang S, Lee S et al.
journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
abstract: Chromosome 3q (3q) amplification is a frequent event in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and other cancer types, yet therapeutic strategies targeting oncogenic drivers within this amplicon have been unsuccessful. Our study revealed that the 3q amplicon encodes multiple Golgi-related proteins, including Phospholipase D1 (PLD1), which catalyzes the production of a potential oncogenic lipid, phosphatidic acid. We found that PLD1 is highly expressed in 3q-amplified NSCLC (3q-NSCLC) and its enzymatic activity is further boosted by coamplified PLD1 activator, ARF-like GTPase 14. High PLD1 activity is essential for 3q-NSCLC growth and metastasis. Mechanistically, PLD1 drives secretion of oncogenic factors via the carriers from the trans Golgi network to the cell surface pathway to support tumor growth. Transferrin receptor 1 (TFRC), which encodes a membrane protein, is coamplified with PLD1 and overexpressed in 3q-NSCLC. A TFRC antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) carrying a PLD1 inhibitor exhibited potential antitumor activity in mouse models. These findings establish PLD1 as a promoter of 3q-NSCLC and provide proof of concept for the development of PLD1-targeted therapies, including ADC-based approaches, for this challenging cancer subtype.

title: TRIM22 in cancer: a context-dependent E3 ligase at the interface of interferon, p53, and tumor plasticity.
authors: Qiu C, Dai L
abstract: TRIM22 is a TRIM family E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is strongly induced by interferons. For many years, it has been identified primarily as an antiviral effector, a role that remains well validated. A growing body of cancer-related work now forces us to expand that view considerably. Depending on tumor type, upstream signaling context, and the specific substrates available in a given cell, TRIM22 can either constrain malignancy or actively promote it. In breast, colorectal, ovarian, endometrial, hepatocellular, cervical, and gastric cancers, as well as in certain lung tumor subsets, TRIM22 is frequently downregulated or functionally impaired. Where this occurs, its re-expression tends to curb proliferation, invasion, stemness, and cachexia-associated programs. Conversely, in non-small-cell lung carcinoma, glioblastoma, melanoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, TRIM22 often takes on a pro-tumorigenic role. It drives epithelial mesenchymal transition, NF-κB signaling, autophagy, and acquired resistance to chemotherapy or targeted agents. The substrate repertoire of TRIM22 is remarkably broad. It includes p53-related effectors, I-κBα, NF-κB components, β-catenin, TCF4, CCS-STAT3, PHLPP2, Raf-1, p21, ADRB2, CDT2, and Smad2. In this review, we synthesize recent findings and argue that TRIM22 functions as a stress-responsive ubiquitin signaling hub rather than as a conventional oncogene or tumor suppressor. It integrates inputs from interferons, p53, hormonal cues, and inflammatory pathways. The phenotypic outcome, whether tumor suppression or tumor promotion, is dictated by cellular lineage and the pre-existing molecular wiring. Deciphering this contextual logic is the key to translating TRIM22 biology into clinically useful strategies.

title: Brief Report: Combination Capmatinib and Trametinib in Metastatic MET-Driven NSCLC.
authors: Brown T, Lara MS, Jiang F et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy has improved outcomes in patients with NSCLC harboring MET alterations. Nevertheless, primary and acquired resistance ultimately limit the durability of response. This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of the MET inhibitor capmatinib with the MEK inhibitor trametinib in patients with metastatic MET-driven NSCLC who had progressed on prior treatment with at least one MET inhibitor.
METHODS: A multicenter phase I study evaluated capmatinib in combination with trametinib in patients with advanced-stage NSCLC harboring activating MET alterations and prior exposure to at least one MET TKI. A three-plus-three dose-escalation design was used to assess the safety and tolerability of the combination.
RESULTS: Three patients (N = 3) were enrolled in the study and completed a median of three cycles of therapy. Dose-limiting toxicities, including rash, edema, and nausea, necessitated dose reductions in the first two patients and the initiation of therapy in the third patient at a lower dose level. Ultimately, all patients discontinued therapy because of treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). The study was terminated early because of poor accrual and TRAEs. No radiographic objective responses were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: In this phase I trial, capmatinib plus trametinib was associated with marked TRAEs, and treatment was discontinued in all participants. On the basis of these findings, further investigation of this combination of MET and MEK inhibitors at the tested dose levels is not recommended. Future studies, if pursued, should consider modified dosing strategies, alternative MET and MEK inhibitor combinations, and MET-altered tumors with evidence of MAPK-mediated resistance.

title: Becotatug Vedotin + Pucotenlimab+Platinum Induction and Sequential CCRT for Unresectable LA NSCLC
summary: This is a prospective, single-arm phase II clinical study enrolling patients with locally advanced unresectable non-small cell lung cancer. All enrolled patients receive induction therapy with Becotatug Vedotin combined with pucotenlimab and platinum-based regimens. Patients who complete the scheduled induction treatment will subsequently receive definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy.

title: Vibostolimab Coformulated with Pembrolizumab Plus Chemotherapy as First-Line Therapy for Extensive-Stage Small-Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Sands J, Lu S, Aerts JG et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vibostolimab, an anti-T-cell immunoreceptor with immunoglobulin and ITIM domains (TIGIT) antibody, showed antitumor activity with pembrolizumab in non-small-cell lung cancer.
OBJECTIVE: The KEYVIBE-008 study evaluated vibostolimab coformulated with pembrolizumab (vibostolimab/pembrolizumab) plus etoposide and platinum-based chemotherapy (EP) versus atezolizumab plus EP as first-line therapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer.
METHODS: Participants aged ≥18 years with untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer were randomized 1:1 to vibostolimab/pembrolizumab (200 mg each) or atezolizumab (1200 mg) every 3 weeks, with EP and cisplatin/carboplatin for the first four cycles. The primary endpoint was overall survival. The prespecified interim analysis included a non-binding futility analysis of overall survival (futility threshold for actual number of events, P = 0.4816).
RESULTS: Four hundred and sixty participants were randomized (both arms, n = 230). Median time from randomization to data cutoff (4 June, 2024) was 16.6 (range 11.3‒26.1) months. The prespecified futility criterion for overall survival was met (hazard ratio 1.26; 95% confidence interval 1.00‒1.59; P = 0.9762). There was no difference in progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.01; 95% confidence interval 0.82‒1.23) or objective response rates (71.7% with vibostolimab/pembrolizumab vs 74.8% with atezolizumab). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 66.8% of participants treated with vibostolimab/pembrolizumab and 57.2% treated with atezolizumab. Immune-mediated adverse events and infusion reactions occurred in 39.3% and 29.7% of participants, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: In this interim analysis of vibostolimab/pembrolizumab plus EP versus atezolizumab plus EP as first-line therapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, the prespecified futility criterion for overall survival was met. Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events and immune-mediated adverse events were more frequent with vibostolimab/pembrolizumab versus atezolizumab. Given the overall benefit/risk profile, treatment with vibostolimab/pembrolizumab was discontinued.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov, NCT05224141.

title: Impact of Opt-Out Versus Opt-In Recruitment on Engagement of FDNY WTC-Exposed Responders in a Tobacco Cessation Intervention.
authors: Moline T, Mueller AK, Prezant DJ et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: World Trade Center (WTC)-exposed Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) rescue/recovery workers have an elevated risk of smoking-related morbidity. Despite access to free tobacco cessation treatment, some individuals in this population continue to smoke. In other settings, opt-out treatment approaches increase treatment initiation, but effectiveness in occupational health programs is unclear. Accordingly, we (1) assessed whether an opt-out strategy increases engagement with a Tobacco Cessation Program and (2) identified factors associated with engagement.
METHODS: This was a randomized trial among FDNY firefighters and Emergency Medical Service (EMS) who self-reported smoking and were eligible for the WTC Health Program Lung Cancer Screening Program. 1:1 randomization occurred prior to contact for opt-out recruitment with Enhanced Care treatment (Opt-Out/Enhanced) or opt-in recruitment with Standard Care treatment (Opt-In/Standard). Opt-Out/Enhanced included proactive outreach and tailored biofeedback during counseling; Opt-In/Standard included participant-initiated engagement and standard counseling. Both groups were offered identical no-cost pharmacotherapy (varenicline). Engagement was defined as: consented enrollment (expressed interest and provided informed consent) and treatment initiation (attendance at ≥1 counseling session). Engagement differences were evaluated using logistic regression; sociodemographic and health-related factors were characterized descriptively without formal testing due to small numbers.
RESULTS: Overall, 312 individuals were randomized (Opt-Out/Enhanced, n = 156 and Opt-In/Standard, n = 156). Engagement was low (7.4%). Consented enrollment (n = 23; OR = 3.05; 95% CI = 1.11-9.72) and treatment initiation (n = 18; OR = 2.08; 95% CI = 0.72-6.73) were higher in Opt-Out/Enhanced versus Opt-In/Standard. Treatment initiators had a median age of 60.5 (vs 65.0 years among non-initiators); 38.9% were EMS (vs 18.0%), 22.2% were female (vs 6.9%), 77.8% had a prior cessation attempt (vs 23.5%), and 55.6% had abnormal lung function (vs 32.9%). Participants were too few to analyze cessation outcomes in depth.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite low engagement overall, opt-out treatment had higher engagement with tobacco cessation treatment. This supports other work that has found opt-out treatment to be encouraged for hard-to-reach populations.

title: Marijuana (Cannabis) Smoking Increases the Risk of Lung Cancer: Evidence from a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Karimi M, Kazemi K, Pourhanifeh MH et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Marijuana (cannabis) use has become increasingly prevalent worldwide, raising concerns about its potential long-term health effects, particularly on the respiratory system. While tobacco smoking is a well-established risk factor for lung cancer,the association between cannabis use and lung cancer risk remains unclear and controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis of existing observational studies aimed to evaluate the potential relationship between marijuana use and the risk ofdeveloping lung cancer.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus to identify cohort and case-controlstudies up to September 2025. Studies were selected, relevant data were extracted, and statistically analyzed using effect sizes (ES)and 95% confidence intervals (CI). All analyses were conducted using STATA software.
FINDINGS: This meta-analysis included six observational studies, comprising 16 effect sizes, consisting of two cohort studies andfour case-control studies. The pooled analysis of the cohort studies (7 effect sizes) indicated a statistically significant associationbetween marijuana (cannabis) smoking and increased lung cancer risk (ES: 2.06; 95% CI: [1.04-4.07]; P=0.038; I2=75%). Incontrast, the meta-analysis of the case-control studies (9 effect sizes) showed a non-significant increase in risk (ES: 1.16; 95% CI:[0.71-1.88]; P=0.542; I2=82%).
CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis indicates that marijuana smoking may increase lung cancer risk, with cohort studies showing asignificant twofold association. Although case-control studies were not statistically significant, the upward trend highlights theimportance of considering cannabis use in lung cancer risk assessments and patient counseling.

title: Efficacy and safety of single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for the curative treatment of extracranial primary Tumors: A collaborative systematic review on behalf of the SBRT Focus Group of the European Society for Radiotherapy & Oncology (ESTRO).
authors: Cuccia F, Franzese C, Dubash S et al.
abstract: Single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SF-SBRT) represents one of the most advanced frontiers in modern radiation oncology. While ultra-hypofractionation has entered everyday clinical practice in different fields of the oncological care, curative treatments in one session are increasingly attractive for the potential favorable combination of logistic advantages with safety and clinical outcomes. This collaborative systematic review promoted by the ESTRO SBRT Focus Group in participation with members of different disease-site Focus Groups collects the available data in support of SF-SBRT for the curative treatment of the main extracranial primary tumors. The findings highlight that, for specific anatomical sites, SF-SBRT is both safe and effective though the results emphasize the critical importance of careful patient selection and mandatory technological requirements for treatment planning and delivery. This collaborative work provides a comprehensive overview of current evidence and identifies key knowledge gaps for future investigation and upcoming clinical trials.

title: Effects of enhanced recovery after surgery and prehabilitation interventions on postoperative outcomes after lung resection in patients with lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Kim D, Shin G
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lung resection is the standard curative treatment for resectable lung cancer; however, postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) and prolonged hospital length of stay (LOS) remain major barriers to recovery and healthcare efficiency. Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) and prehabilitation are distinct perioperative strategies that differ in their timing, intervention components, and mechanisms of action, but both aim to optimize patients' perioperative condition and improve postoperative recovery. However, their effectiveness compared with conventional perioperative care based solely on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) has not been comprehensively synthesized.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of ERAS and prehabilitation in reducing PPCs, shortening LOS, and improving patient-reported outcomes following pulmonary resection for lung cancer.
SUBJECTS AND METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs involving adults undergoing pulmonary resection for primary lung cancer. Searches of PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL Complete, RISS, KISS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform identified studies published between January 2015 and May 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled odds ratios (ORs) for PPCs and mean differences (MDs) for LOS. Patient-reported outcomes were synthesized narratively according to the SWiM guideline.
RESULTS: Ten RCTs involving 1,569 participants met the inclusion criteria. ERAS and prehabilitation significantly reduced PPCs compared with conventional perioperative care (OR = 0.48, 95% CI = 0.36-0.65, p < 0.001). The exploratory pooled analysis suggested a shorter postoperative LOS (MD = -2.30 days, 95% CI = -3.58 to -1.01); however, heterogeneity was considerable (I 2 = 97.9%), and the 95% prediction interval crossed the null. Narrative synthesis demonstrated consistent improvements in anxiety, depression, postoperative pain, pulmonary function, quality of life, and functional recovery.
CONCLUSION: ERAS and prehabilitation are effective perioperative strategies for improving outcomes after pulmonary resection for lung cancer. Their implementation in routine clinical practice may reduce postoperative complications, accelerate recovery, and improve healthcare efficiency. Further multicenter RCTs are needed to optimize intervention components, standardize outcome measures, and strengthen evidence for long-term and patient-reported outcomes.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: CRD420261373242.

title: Dexmedetomidine-based opioid-sparing anesthesia in video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
authors: Hsieh KW, Wen CH, Chen CH
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dexmedetomidine has increasingly been incorporated into opioid-sparing anesthetic strategies during video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) because of its analgesic properties and minimal respiratory depression. However, dexmedetomidine remains associated with dose-related hemodynamic adverse effects, particularly bradycardia and hypotension. We evaluated whether a reduced-dose dexmedetomidine regimen decreases intraoperative opioid requirements while maintaining acceptable hemodynamic safety during VATS.
METHODS: In this prospective randomized controlled trial, 68 patients undergoing VATS were randomly assigned to either a dexmedetomidine group or a control group (34 patients each). The dexmedetomidine group received a loading dose of 0.5 µg/kg followed by continuous infusion at 0.5 µg/kg/h during surgery. The control group received conventional fentanyl-based anesthesia. The primary outcome was maintenance-phase rescue fentanyl consumption. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), postoperative respiratory complications, and perioperative safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Maintenance-phase rescue fentanyl consumption was significantly lower in the dexmedetomidine group than in the control group (18.7 vs. 33.2 µg, P = 0.009). Postoperative pain scores, rescue analgesic requirements, PONV, and respiratory complications were comparable between groups. However, the dexmedetomidine group demonstrated a higher incidence of intraoperative bradycardia (23.5% vs. 0%, P = 0.005) and postoperative hypotension during PACU stay (23.5% vs. 2.9%, P = 0.027). These hemodynamic events were transient and responsive to pharmacologic intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Dexmedetomidine-based opioid-sparing anesthesia reduced maintenance-phase rescue fentanyl administration during VATS. However, the reduction was modest, was not associated with clear postoperative benefits, and was accompanied by increased bradycardia and hypotension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05431322), registered on 14 June 2022. Available at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05431322 .

title: [Evolution of Perioperative Immunotherapy Paradigms in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer: From Adjuvant Dilemma to Neoadjuvant Priority].
authors: Xu J, Jiang Z
abstract: The application of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has reshaped the perioperative treatment pattern of resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Currently, three treatment paradigms have emerged: adjuvant, neoadjuvant alone, and 'sandwich' (neoadjuvant+surgery+adjuvant). Although IMpower010 and KEYNOTE-091 achieved positive results in adjuvant immunotherapy, the negative results of two large phase III studies, BR.31 and ANVIL, raised questions about the generalizability of this model. In contrast, neoadjuvant immunotherapy has shown efficacy in multiple phase III studies. This advantage may stem from the preservation of the intact tumor antigen repertoire and draining lymph node architecture, enabling chemo-immunotherapy to elicit more robust systemic immune responses. Currently, both neoadjuvant alone and 'sandwich' models are recommended by guidelines, but the 5-year overall survival (OS) rates of CheckMate-816 and KEYNOTE-671 are nearly identical (65.4% vs 64.6%), and the pathological complete response (pCR) rate of CheckMate-77T (25.3%) is comparable to that of CheckMate-816 (24%), suggesting that the incremental benefit of extending neoadjuvant cycles and adding postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy in the 'sandwich' model is very limited. In the future, an individualized decision-making model based on pCR and molecular residual disease (MRD) status, such as de-escalation to observation for those achieving pCR with negative MRD, and intensification for those with residual disease or positive MRD, is expected to optimize the balance between treatment intensity and survival benefit. In summary, the existing evidence favors the adoption of a 'neoadjuvant first' strategy for resectable NSCLC. Based mainly on cross-trial indirect comparisons, the neoadjuvant alone model offers comparable efficacy to the 'sandwich' approach with potential cost-effectiveness advantages, and may be preferred as the initial strategy. Individualized post-neoadjuvant management represents the future direction of this field. .

title: Exhaled Breath Analysis for Lung Cancer Detection: From VOCs Signatures to EBC-Based Liquid Biopsy and Clinical Translation.
authors: Sun P, Fu Z, Wang S et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally. Although low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is the current standard for early screening, its high false-positive rates and cumulative radiation exposure create a pressing clinical need for complementary, non-invasive diagnostic tools. Exhaled breath analysis represents an accessible strategy for early detection and risk stratification. Early breathomics primarily focused on gas-phase volatile organic compounds (VOCs). However, as volatile metabolites, VOCs are chemically unstable and highly susceptible to background ambient air and physiological confounders. Distinct from gas-phase analysis, exhaled breath condensate (EBC) offers enhanced biomarker stability and functions as a lung-proximal liquid biopsy. By capturing non-volatile, high-molecular-weight analytes, including tumor-derived nucleic acids and proteins, EBC more closely reflects the underlying molecular mechanisms of the respiratory microenvironment. Nevertheless, the clinical translation of EBC remains constrained by severe sample dilution, unstandardized collection device architectures, and pre-analytical inconsistencies. This review summarizes the progression from VOCs profiling to EBC-based platforms, detailing recent advances in sample harvesting, ultrasensitive detection technologies, and multi-omics integration. Advancing EBC toward routine clinical use requires consensus-driven standard operating procedures and the application of machine learning algorithms to high-dimensional datasets. Future efforts should prioritize large-scale, multicenter prospective trials to validate specific EBC signatures, thereby establishing this technology as a reliable liquid biopsy for precision pulmonary oncology.

title: Nurses' perspectives on perioperative pulmonary rehabilitation for patients with lung cancer in the pre-implementation phase: a CFIR 2.0-guided study.
authors: Yang C, Liu Y, Li F et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite strong evidence supporting perioperative pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) for patients undergoing lung cancer surgery, little is known about factors that may influence implementation prior to program rollout, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Guided by the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0), this study aimed to identify anticipated barriers and facilitators to inform program refinement and future implementation strategies.
METHODS: A descriptive qualitative design was used. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nurses from the thoracic surgery department of a tertiary hospital in China (September-November 2025). Guided by the four CFIR 2.0 domains (innovation, outer setting, inner setting, individuals), directed content analysis was performed based on nurses' perspectives.
RESULTS: Sixteen nurses were interviewed, representing diverse roles: Ward/ICU frontline staff nurses, charge nurses, unit secretaries, administrative nurses and nurse managers. Relevant constructs included 22 of the 29 CFIR 2.0 constructs and 8 subconstructs. Facilitators spanned: innovation (source, evidence base, relative advantage, trialability); outer setting (financing, policy, external pressure); inner setting (relational connections, communication, culture, incentive systems); and individual factors (team needs, leadership/practitioner capability, motivation). Barriers comprised: innovation (adaptability, complexity, cost); outer setting (local condition, partnerships and connections); inner setting (structural characteristics, compatibility, access to knowledge and information); and individuals (recipient needs, capability). Notably, implementation concerns differed across nursing roles, reflecting role heterogeneity and underscoring the need for tailored implementation strategies.
CONCLUSION: Implementation of perioperative PR for patients undergoing lung cancer surgery is influenced by multilevel factors spanning innovation, outer setting, inner setting, and individuals determinants. Differences in concerns across nursing roles highlight the importance of role-tailored implementation strategies. These findings provide a foundation for optimizing implementation approaches and may facilitate the sustainable integration of evidence-based PR into routine practice, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare settings.

title: Localized hydrogel depots for CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors: materials design, cellular fitness and translational deployment.
authors: Zhao J, Zhang Y, Wei Z et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is less effective in solid tumors than in selected hematologic malignancies because vascular, stromal, spatial, and immunosuppressive barriers restrict cell delivery and function. Local hydrogels and related biomaterials can convert a transient administration into a spatially organized depot, but their benefit depends on more than polymer identity. This review therefore combines a scenario-driven framework-depot versus bolus, intratumoral versus peritumoral placement, unresected versus postsurgical disease, and cell-loaded versus cell-free support-with a materials-centered analysis of formation, administration, time-dependent mechanics, architecture, degradation, biochemical presentation, and manufacturing. Direct evidence is distinguished from adjacent mechanistic evidence and design hypotheses. Across the available studies, the best-supported functions are improved delivered-cell recovery, regional persistence, controlled presentation of supportive cues, and enhanced antitumor activity in selected preclinical models. By contrast, universal material-property optima, clinically validated hydrogel-CAR-T products, and cryopreservation of a final cell-loaded depot have not been established. We define practical tests for gelation and device compatibility, productive egression, material-to-cell fitness, component attribution, and integrated-product safety. A materials-focused comparative table and a 30-study evidence map separate measured values from inferred mechanisms and identify where CAR-T cells were directly loaded, administered separately, manufactured in a matrix, or generated in situ. The resulting framework emphasizes that successful platforms must coordinate material behavior, CAR-T quality, anatomical placement, and clinical workflow rather than maximizing retention or chemical complexity alone.

title: Epigenetic and metabolic plasticity of tumor cells in immunotherapy resistance.
authors: Choi JE, Baek I
abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has demonstrated remarkable efficacy across multiple tumor types. Despite their significant clinical benefits, most patients with solid tumors remain refractory to immunotherapy, and initial responders frequently develop acquired resistance. Tumor plasticity is a key driver of resistance to cancer immunotherapy. In this review, we discuss how epigenetic and metabolic plasticity of tumor contributes to immunotherapy resistance and highlight emerging strategies targeting these programs to overcome resistance and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Application of CAR-T cell therapy in orthopedics: From bone malignancies to non-malignant musculoskeletal disorders.
authors: Que Y, Xie X, Xie W et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed hematologic oncology, but its application in orthopaedic diseases remains at an early stage. In bone malignancies, including osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and bone metastases, antigen heterogeneity, limited trafficking and persistence, and the immunosuppressive skeletal microenvironment restrict efficacy. CAR-engineered approaches are also emerging in non-malignant disorders: CD19-directed CAR-T therapy has shown early clinical activity in refractory rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune rheumatic diseases, whereas senolytic CAR-T strategies for osteoarthritis remain preclinical. This review summarizes current evidence across malignant and non-malignant orthopaedic conditions, with emphasis on target selection, safety, and translational feasibility. Key barriers include antigen escape, impaired infiltration, limited persistence, local immunosuppression, manufacturing complexity, and on-target/off-tumour toxicity. Emerging strategies include multi-target receptors, chemokine receptor engineering, locoregional delivery, safety-control systems, and allogeneic or point-of-care manufacturing. Current evidence supports CAR-T and related CAR-engineered cells as potential complementary approaches for selected refractory orthopaedic conditions, although further translation requires stronger clinical evidence and improved biological and manufacturing strategies. The Translational Potential of this Article: This review identifies disease-specific targets, barriers, and engineering priorities relevant to translating CAR-engineered cell therapies into orthopaedic practice. These considerations may inform preclinical validation and early-phase trials in refractory bone malignancies and selected non-malignant musculoskeletal disorders.

title: Why only 3 months? Immunological constraints on CAR-T therapy in gastrointestinal cancers.
authors: Zeng L, Wei S, Chen N et al.
abstract: In June 2026, satri-cel/CT041, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product targeting Claudin18.2, received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration for the treatment of Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after failure of at least two prior lines of therapy. This marks the first CAR-T product approved worldwide for solid tumours. The approval ends the long-standing debate over whether CAR-T cells can be effective against solid malignancies, yet it simultaneously raises a more pointed issue: in its pivotal randomised controlled trial, median progression-free survival was 3.25 months (95% CI 2.86-4.53) with satri-cel against 1.77 months (95% CI 1.61-2.04) with treatment of physician's choice, giving a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24-0.56). The two medians differ by 1.48 months; that figure marks where each survival distribution is cut in half and is not the benefit any individual patient can expect, and approval does not equate to a cure. Taking this as a starting point, this review systematically dissects the immunological bottlenecks that constrain CAR-T efficacy in gastrointestinal tumours. We first trace the evidence chain from phase I studies through the randomised controlled trial to exploratory adjuvant-therapy settings and then integrate the landscape of targets-Claudin18.2, glypican-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, mesothelin, and CDH17-within a target-tumour matrix encompassing gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer. The core section focuses on four intertwined immunological constraints: spatiotemporal heterogeneity and escape at the antigen level; a therapeutic window shaped jointly by epitope masking within tight junctions and immune privilege of the gastric mucosal stem cell niche-this mechanism not only explains why Claudin18.2-directed CAR-T cells exhibit an acceptable safety profile despite target expression on normal tissues but also provides a paradigm for rational selection of next-generation targets; a suppressive microenvironment composed of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumour-associated macrophages, transforming growth factor-β, adenosine, and a hypoxic and acidotic metabolic milieu; and CAR-T exhaustion driven by chronic antigen stimulation. We particularly emphasise that metabolic stress and exhaustion are not two parallel obstacles. We put forward a mechanistic model in which persistent antigen stimulation combined with intratumoral hypoxia acts as a "double hit": through mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, the two inputs raise nuclear factor of activated T-cell (NFAT) activity and so drive the TOX/NR4A-dominated exhaustion program. This model is assembled from chronic-infection and mouse tumour systems and has not been tested in human CAR-T cells or in satri-cel-treated patients. We advance it as a framework for organising the four bottlenecks and for explaining why single-point interventions struggle to lift the efficacy ceiling, not as a demonstrated account. On this basis, we discuss strategies such as armouring, logic gating, transcription factor engineering, gene editing, and chemokine receptor modification, along with combination regimens involving checkpoint inhibition, oncolytic viruses, locoregional administration, and microbiome modulation, and we evaluate alternative platforms including CAR-macrophages, CAR-NK cells, and in vivo CAR-T generation. The watershed has been crossed, but the work of turning 3 months into 30 has only just begun.
